metadata.title: The impact of schooling on trust in political institutions – Differences arising from students' immigration backgrounds

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 microdata and analyzes a subsample from North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Germany, focusing on one randomly selected Year Eight class per participating school. The authors report that the data were weighted by strata and that weights and Jackknife sampling variables were employed in analyses conducted via the IDB Analyzer to correct for sampling error and attenuate p-value underestimation. For Germany, stratification for selecting classes used school type (secondary school track system) and the proportion of students with migration backgrounds in school (more vs. less than 30%). The manuscript does not name the exact weight variable(s), but the use of IDB Analyzer macros with jackknife variables indicates complex survey design handling consistent with ICCS technical documentation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are scale scores (TIPI, student-teacher/student-student relationships, victimisation, national identity) and a civic knowledge test score based on ICCS-provided Weighted Likelihood Estimations (WLE). The paper does not describe an explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation) for missing questionnaire/test responses, so missing-data handling is not documented. Given the ICCS design and the use of IDB Analyzer macros, missingness is likely handled within the IEA estimation procedures, but the authors do not report the specific approach.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analyses use the ICCS 2016 subsample from North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Germany. ICCS was configured to sample students in the grade corresponding to average age 13.5 years (Year Eight in Germany); in each selected participating school, one Year Eight class was randomly selected and assessed. The analytic sample consists of 1451 students in 59 secondary schools with written guardian consent. The immigration-background variable is constructed from three items (student and/or guardians born outside the country): First Generation (N=69), Second Generation (N=504), and Non-Immigrant (N=878). The First Generation group is omitted from regression analytics due to its small size, while descriptive statistics are reported for it; regressions compare Non-Immigrant vs. Second Generation and also estimate models for all students combined.

main_findings.target_variable: predicts TIPI for non-immigrant students but not for students with immigration
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 the study leveraged Immigration background group, Gender, Socioeconomic status (SES) to predict predicts TIPI for non-immigrant students but not for students with immigration, finding that This study uses ICCS 2016 data from North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), Germany, focusing on Year Eight students (N=1451 in 59 secondary schools). Trust in Political Institutions (TIPI) is measured with six Likert items and analyzed as a continuous scale score; civic knowledge is a timed test scored using ICCS-provided Weighted Likelihood Estimations (WLE) from Rasch partial credit models. The authors estimate weighted regression models (via IDB Analyzer) with jackknife sampling variables to account for ICCS complex survey design and stratification by school type and migration-background composition. They report that student-teacher and student-student relationship quality are positive predictors of TIPI, with stronger associations among students with immigration backgrounds, while victimisation is not a significant predictor. Civic knowledge predicts TIPI for non-immigrant students but not for students with immigration backgrounds, and national identity predicts TIPI in both groups with a stronger effect among students with immigration backgrounds. The analysis is cross-sectional, so causal claims cannot be made, and the paper does not document an explicit missing-data handling procedure. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical regression-based study using ICCS 2016 scale scores and WLE-based civic knowledge, but it does not train or compare machine learning predictive models (no ML algorithms are reported). Consequently, ml_techniques are empty and main_findings are not populated under the ML/predictive schema requirement. The study’s results are presented as weighted linear regression coefficients and explained variance (R²), which are outside the ML-only extraction target of this schema.
